interest: Shows 1930s Japanese labor disputes, including chimney-sitting protests and GM/Singer strikes, amid growing state suppression of leftist unions.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.5045, covering April 21, 1930 to September 18, 1935) documents labor unrest, strikes, and lockouts in Japan during the Great Depression and the subsequent rise of nationalistic militarism. Recorded through diplomatic despatches, periodic political report extracts, consular despatches, and telegrams from the U.S. Embassy and Consulate General in Tokyo, the file details major industrial disputes across municipal transit, textile manufacturing, automotive assembly, and retail sales. Prominent cases include the April 1930 and September–October 1934 Tokyo municipal streetcar and bus strikes, the 53-day Kanegafuchi Spinning Company strike, violent clashes at General Motors Japan in 1931, an extensive dispute at the Singer Sewing Machine Company over installment collections and union recognition, and novel protest tactics such as prolonged endurance 'chimney sitting.' The records highlight the role of the Metropolitan Police Board in mediating disputes and imposing compulsory arbitration under the Labor Disputes Arbitration Law, the significant financial impact of traditional discharge allowances, the lack of formal legal status for Japanese labor unions, and the gradual decline in dispute numbers by 1934–1935 amid rising nationalism and the suppression of leftist labor organizations.

subfiles.about: Initial telegraphic report on the municipal streetcar and bus strike in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 69: Castle reports a Tokyo streetcar and bus strike partly paralyzing transit, with volunteer operators maintaining limited service and no violence or political involvement.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 69 from Castle on Tokyo streetcar and bus strike

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note recording Despatch No. 127 on strikes during April 1930.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a May 1930 report on April streetcar strikes in Tokyo and Kobe.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 127 regarding April 1930 strikes

subfiles.about: Embassy report extract detailing the streetcar and bus strikes in Tokyo and Kobe in April 1930.
subfiles.summary: April 1930 Tokyo transit strike: over 10,000 streetcar/bus operators protested bonus cuts but collapsed quickly for lack of public sympathy and use of volunteers; in Kobe, about 1,000 of 1,300 workers struck over a reinstatement demand and failed to win it.
subfiles.title: Report extract on Tokyo and Kobe streetcar and bus strikes of April 1930

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 189 on the settlement of textile mill strikes.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a July 1930 report on the end of strikes at three Kanegafuchi Spinning Company mills.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 189 on Kanegafuchi Spinning Company strikes

subfiles.about: Embassy report extract outlining the settlement terms of the 53-day strikes at Kanegafuchi Spinning Company mills.
subfiles.summary: 53-day Kanegafuchi Spinning strikes ended at Hyogo, Osaka, and Kyoto mills: Hyogo folded a 30% wartime allowance into wages, cut rents, and dissolved strike headquarters and union branches, while Osaka and Kyoto workers were paid from company funds, with a Diet labor member calling it a draw.
subfiles.title: Report extract on settlement of Kanegafuchi Spinning Company strikes

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 240 regarding strikes in Asakusa, Osaka, and Fukuoka.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a June 1931 report on strikes at Japan Dyeing, Sumitomo Steel Works, and a Fukuoka coal mine.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 240 on May 1931 strikes

subfiles.about: Embassy report extract on endurance chimney-sitting and underground mine sit-ins as strike tactics.
subfiles.summary: Report: 'chimney-sitting' strikes spread after a 130-hour Kawasaki protest; Hiroshi Chiba held 12 days atop a smokestack at Japan Dyeing, prompting Sumitomo Steel to cut its ladders, while 200 Fukuoka miners stayed underground 125 hours before a compromise.
subfiles.title: Report extract on chimney-sitting and sit-down strikes in Asakusa, Osaka, and Fukuoka

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note recording Despatch No. 324 on 1931 labor statistics and the General Motors dispute.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a September 1931 report on rising labor disputes and violence at General Motors Japan injuring two foreign staff.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 324 on labor statistics and General Motors dispute

subfiles.about: Embassy report extract detailing depression-era labor dispute statistics and violent clashes during the General Motors Japan strike.
subfiles.summary: Report: Social Bureau statistics show labor disputes rising sharply in the Depression (2,289 in 1930, 1,079 in early 1931); at General Motors Japan, strikers injured an American and a Dane on August 22, 1931, and clashed with police on August 28.
subfiles.title: Report extract on 1931 labor dispute statistics and General Motors strike violence

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 195 on the Singer Sewing Machine Company strike.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Grew's November 1932 report on a strike by Singer Sewing Machine Company agents and employees in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 195 on Singer Sewing Machine Company strike

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch concerning Singer Sewing Machine Company's appeals for Embassy assistance during an employee strike.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Singer agents refused to surrender machines and installment payments during a strike; with legal action impractical and police reluctant to intervene, the Embassy held informal Foreign Office talks prompting Home Department mediation, with no basis for formal diplomatic action.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 195 from Grew on Singer Sewing Machine Company difficulties

subfiles.about: Company statement defending its installment business model and refusing the demands of the All-Japan Singer Union.
subfiles.summary: The Singer Sewing Machine Company provides a comprehensive 12-page defense of its 32-year operations in Japan against a nationwide strike organized by the 'All-Japan Singer Union.' The company refutes the union's five demands—capping retail prices, creating retirement allowances, altering commission contracts, handing over fidelity insurance policies, and restricting employee discharges—arguing they would destroy its hire-purchase credit model. Emphasizing severe exchange losses resulting from the yen's drop from $0.50 to $0.21, the company accuses radical agitators of coercion and warns it will terminate operations in Japan entirely rather than surrender to outside union pressure.
subfiles.title: Statement of the Singer Sewing Machine Company regarding the All-Japan Singer Union strike
subfiles.to: Embassy Tokyo / Japanese Employees / General Public

subfiles.about: Consular despatch on the outbreak, organization, and compulsory arbitration of the Tokyo tram and bus strike.
subfiles.summary: Garrels reports a September 1934 strike by 10,200 Tokyo Traffic Labor Union members against 20-48% wage cuts; well-funded and orderly, it ran alongside 70% service by officials and volunteers until the Police Board invoked compulsory arbitration, prompting a September 18 suspension.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 908 from Garrels on Tokyo tram and bus strike

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum evaluating Tokyo Consulate General Despatch No. 922.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (WTT / DLY)
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch No. 922: drafted by a Japanese consular staffer, it merely recounts the Tokyo tram and bus strike settlement and is deemed of no particular interest to the Department.
subfiles.title: State Department memorandum on Despatch No. 922 regarding Tokyo transit strike

subfiles.about: Consular despatch describing the resumed strike, police mediation, and settlement of the Tokyo transit dispute.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Garrels details the resumption of the Tokyo transit strike on October 7 after union leaders rejected a 20 percent wage reduction compromise formulated by the arbitration committee. Facing financial exhaustion, police pressure, and internal defections, the strikers accepted the personal mediation of the Superintendent of the Metropolitan Police Board, concluding a memorandum on October 13 that represented a defeat for the union on wage cuts and strike leader reinstatements. Garrels notes the ironic outcome where 89 percent of workers chose the Electric Bureau's original dismissal plan over the compromise to collect lucrative traditional discharge allowances averaging ¥2,000 each.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 922 from Garrels on settlement of Tokyo tram and bus strike

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 1007 on the September 1934 Tokyo transit strike.
subfiles.summary: Indexes an October 1934 report cross-referencing the major Tokyo tram and bus strike of September 1934.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 1007 on Tokyo transit strike

subfiles.about: Embassy periodic report extract summarizing the September 1934 Tokyo municipal transit strike and arbitration.
subfiles.summary: Report: a 12-day strike by 10,200 Tokyo tram and bus workers against wage cuts and dismissals stayed orderly until the Police Board compelled arbitration, suspending the strike September 17 amid strong union resistance and fears of renewal.
subfiles.title: Report extract on Tokyo tram and bus strike of September 1934

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 1475 on labor dispute statistics from 1930 to 1934.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a September 1935 report on declining Japanese labor dispute statistics from 1930 to 1934.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 1475 on Japanese labor dispute statistics 1930-1934

subfiles.about: Embassy periodic report extract citing official statistics showing a declining trend in Japanese labor disputes from 1930 to 1934.
subfiles.summary: Report: Japan Times statistics show labor disputes falling from 2,456 in 1931 to 1,915 in 1934, and participants from 191,838 to 120,307, attributed to rising nationalism and the suppression of leftist labor organizations.
subfiles.title: Report extract on Japanese labor dispute statistics 1930-1934 and rising nationalism
